commenti.body:
Other Side of the Wind?!

He was his own enemy, to some extent. in some of his projects (Ambersons, Touch of Evil, maybe others) filming went smoothly and then he spent months editing and nitpicking, he was so much a perfectionist that it was nearly impossible for him to finish any project and that made people wary of giving him money.

Despite all the problems he had in financing and completing movies in later years, he completed ***A Touch of Evil*** with Charlton Heston and himself, ***The Trial*** with Anthony Perkins and ***Chimes at Midnight*** starring himself, as well as some great docu work like ***F for Fake***. He also starred as Harry Lime in ***The Third Man***, one of the all time greatest noir roles. 

So while we might feel sad at the roads not taken there is still an incredible legacy of great work for us to enjoy. 

Who here agrees that ***Chimes at Midnight*** is the best Shakespeare adaptation ever?
Chimes, Ran, and Throne of Blood I’d have as the top 3 Shakespeare adaptations. Welles’ Othello and Zeffirelli’s Romeo and Juliet I’d place at a level just under those.
Definitely agree on that selection tho I've never seen the Zeffirelli.

>Who here agrees that *Chimes at Midnight* is the best Shakespeare adaptation ever?

I do!

I think in a very close second is the Russian *Gamlet* (*Hamlet*) (1964).  Brilliant adaptation, and supposedly Shakespeare devotees Kenneth Branagh and John Gielgud consider it the definitive *Hamlet* adaptation.

Of course *Ran* (1985) and *Throne of Blood* (1957) are high up there, but I'm a bit torn on how to count them.  *Gamlet* preserves the full story and setting, only changing the language, whereas *Ran* uses *King Lear* (and an historical episode) as a jumping off-point.

Either way, I think *Chimes at Midnight* is the best, with a lot of great ones up there as well.
I'd only put Ran above it. And as you say, his legacy would be great with just his direction or his acting, he got both.

>Critic Gary Giddens put it well:  
  
*For here is the crux of the Welles conundrum, boiled down to one question: Which is the more impressive feat? A gifted young man is given a film studio, its technicians, and almost unlimited funds to make any movie he desires, and he comes up with Citizen Kane. A mature, experienced, stubbornly individual artist in middle age, working with little more than rent money and spit, makes Chimes at Midnight. The first film revolutionized cinema, yet merely hints at the sublimity of the later work. The question implies \[...\] that the Welles debate has shifted ground. It used to center on the cause of his decline: was the fault in Welles, the stars, the system? Now the decline itself is in question.*
are you saying that Orson Welles never had a decline?

Not in the quality of his work. I think *Chimes* is a great film. Welles also felt it was his best. “Late Welles” is extraordinary. 

In terms of popular success and Hollywood reputation, there was an obvious decline. He struggled for funding — as I’m sure you know, given the research for this post. He was blacklisted and maligned, but his work continued to be remarkable and he continued to hone his craft.
